blocks.text: The previous topic mentioned that a model never sees your raw text directly, only a tokenized version of it, this topic covers exactly what a token is, how tokenization actually splits text, and the very real practical consequences this has for cost, limits, and prompt design.

This topic covers subword tokenization, why one word can become several tokens, how token counts affect both cost and context limits, and small wording choices that shift how many tokens a prompt actually consumes.
1. What a Token Actually Is
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473063656-583230980.png

A token is a chunk of text, sometimes a whole word, sometimes just part of one, that a model tokenizer treats as a single unit, tokens, not words or characters, are the actual unit the model processes and generates.
2. Words Often Split Into Multiple Tokens

blocks.alt: Words Often Split Into Multiple Tokens
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473063657-362721837.png

A word like unbelievable might get split into several smaller tokens, un, believ, able, rather than staying as one unit, this subword approach lets a model handle rare or unfamiliar words by combining familiar smaller pieces, instead of needing every possible whole word memorized as its own token.

code.content:
# Illustrative example, actual splits depend on the specific tokenizer
"unbelievable" -> ["un", "believ", "able"]
"cat"          -> ["cat"]
"cats"         -> ["cat", "s"]

blocks.text: 3. How Subword Tokenization Actually Works
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473063658-271593517.png

Most modern tokenizers use an algorithm like byte pair encoding, which learns a fixed vocabulary of frequent character sequences from a large body of training text, common sequences become single tokens, rarer sequences get broken into smaller, more frequent pieces.
4. Common Words Cost Fewer Tokens Than Rare Ones

blocks.alt: Common Words Cost Fewer Tokens Than Rare Ones
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473063658-128536013.png

Since tokenizer vocabularies are built from frequency in training data, common English words typically map to a single token, rare words, technical jargon, and text in less common languages often split into several tokens, this means the same idea expressed in different languages or vocabulary can consume noticeably different token counts.

blocks.text: 5. Token Counts Directly Affect Cost
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473063659-209539332.png

Most commercial model APIs, covered in depth in the LLM APIs Fundamentals module later in this course, charge based on the number of tokens processed, both the prompt tokens sent in and the response tokens generated, a longer or less token efficient prompt has a direct, measurable cost impact at scale.
6. Token Limits and the Risk of Truncation

blocks.alt: Token Limits and the Risk of Truncation
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473063659-73116902.png

Every model has a maximum context window, a hard limit on the total number of tokens it can process at once, covered in the next topic, exceeding that limit typically causes an error or forces truncation, silently cutting off part of the prompt or the conversation history.

blocks.title: Token limits apply to the combined total, not just the new input
blocks.content: A long conversation history, extensive context documents, and the current prompt all count toward the same token limit together, a prompt that worked fine early in a conversation can eventually push the total over the limit as the conversation grows.

blocks.text: 7. Small Wording Changes Shift Token Boundaries

blocks.alt: Small Wording Changes Shift Token Boundaries
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473063660-961141803.png

Capitalization, punctuation, and even spacing can shift exactly where token boundaries fall, "Hello" and "hello" may tokenize differently, and unusual spacing or formatting can sometimes produce more tokens than the same content written more conventionally.

blocks.title: This is a genuinely practical, not just theoretical, concern
blocks.content: Teams building high volume applications sometimes measurably reduce API cost simply by cleaning up unnecessary whitespace or normalizing casing in their prompts, without changing the actual instructions at all.

blocks.text: 8. Practical Implications for Prompt Engineering

Being aware of tokenization helps explain a few practical realities, why extremely verbose prompts cost more and risk hitting context limits sooner, why examples in a different language or unusual formatting can consume more tokens than expected, and why trimming unnecessary text in a prompt is not just about clarity, it directly reduces cost and context usage.
9. Tools for Inspecting Tokenization

Most model providers offer a tokenizer tool or library that shows exactly how a given piece of text gets split into tokens and how many tokens result, using one of these tools directly on your own prompts is the most reliable way to understand actual token usage rather than guessing.
Worked Example

A team building a document summarization feature notices their API costs are higher than expected. Inspecting their prompts with a tokenizer tool reveals they were including large blocks of redundant whitespace and repeated formatting instructions carried over from an earlier draft.

After cleaning up the prompt, removing redundant whitespace and consolidating repeated instructions into a single clear statement, the same functional prompt now uses roughly fifteen percent fewer tokens per request, directly reducing cost at the same request volume with no change in output quality.
Common Mistakes

items: Assuming token count roughly equals word count, when subword tokenization can produce meaningfully different counts
Not accounting for conversation history and context documents when reasoning about whether a prompt fits within the token limit
Leaving unnecessary whitespace, repeated instructions, or verbose phrasing in a prompt that gets sent at high volume
Never actually inspecting real token counts with a tokenizer tool, relying entirely on rough intuition instead

blocks.text: Practice

Take a prompt you have written before, and using any available tokenizer tool, count how many tokens it actually uses, then try rewriting it more concisely while preserving the same instructions, and compare the token count difference.
Key Takeaway

Tokens, not words, are the actual unit a language model processes, subword tokenization means word count is only a rough proxy for token count, and understanding this directly explains real practical concerns around API cost, context window limits, and why concise, well formatted prompts matter beyond just readability.
